Primary outcome For all PICOs, the primary outcome measure was poor functional outcome, which was defined as a mRS score of 3–6. In studies where a Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) score was reported, a GOS 1–3 was used as an equivalent measure. SAH grading In the literature on aSAH, different scales are used for describing the clinical condition on admission, such as the Hunt&Hess scale and World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) scale. , We used the rating scales as described in the cited manuscript. The Hunt&Hess and WFNS scales are explained in . Data analysis L.H. performed data extraction and analysis. In cases where relevant data were not reported in an eligible study, the corresponding author was contacted by the PICO leader. In the case of no response, one of the guideline chairs also contacted the corresponding author. If no answer was received, data were considered as missing. Where feasible, we conducted fixed-effects meta-analyses, estimating heterogeneity using the REML method, provided no substantial heterogeneity was detected. Results are presented as effect estimates with corresponding 95% CIs. Heterogeneity was assessed using the χ 2 test and quantified with the I 2 statistic. When I 2 exceeded 50%, a random-effects model was applied. We also calculated 95% prediction intervals to account for between-study variability. Results are displayed using forest plots. All analyses were performed in R using the meta package. Evaluation of the quality of evidence and formulation of recommendations The risk of bias of each included randomised trial was assessed with the Cochrane RoB2 tool. As recommended, the evidence synthesis did not use a quality “score” threshold but classified overall risk of bias at the study level and then in the aggregate. The results of data analysis were imported into the GRADEpro Guideline Development Tool (McMaster University, 2015; developed by Evidence Prime, Inc.). For each PICO question and each outcome, the following were considered: risk of bias based on the type of available evidence (randomised or observational studies); considerations on inconsistency of results; indirectness of evidence, imprecision of results and other possible bias. LH generated the GRADE evidence profiles/summary of findings tables, which MWG members used to prepare “Evidence-based recommendations,” based on the GRADE approach. The direction, strength and formulation of the recommendations were determined according to the GRADE evidence profiles and the ESO-SOP. , The phrasing of the recommendations was extensively discussed between all MWG members until consensus was reached. Finally, expert consensus-statements were added whenever the PICO group considered that there was insufficient evidence available to provide evidence-based recommendations and where practical guidance is needed for routine clinical practice. Expert consensus statements were modified using the Delphi method until consensus was reached regarding the phrasing of the statement. The expert consensus statements were then sent to all MWG-members for anonymous voting. According to the ESO SOP for guidelines, only those consensus statements that reached a majority of votes are reported in the guideline. Importantly, these expert consensus statements should not be regarded as evidence-based recommendations, since they only reflect the opinion of the writing group. Drafting of the document, revision and approval Each PICO question was addressed in distinct sections, in line with the updated ESO SOP. First, the “Analysis of current evidence” section summarised current pathophysiological considerations followed by a summary and discussion of the results of the identified RCTs and other studies. Second, “Additional information” was added when more details on the studies referred to in the first section were needed to provide information on key subgroup analyses of the included studies, on ongoing or future RCTs, and on other studies which can provide important clinical guidance on the topic. Third, an “Expert consensus statement” paragraph was added whenever the MWG considered that insufficient evidence was available to provide evidence-based recommendations for situations in which practical guidance is needed for everyday clinical practice. The Guideline document was reviewed by all MWG members and modified using a Delphi approach until a consensus was reached. The final submitted document was peer-reviewed by 2 external reviewers, 2 members of the ESO Guideline Board and 1 member of the Executive Committee. Medical (non-)invasive treatment to decrease the risk of rebleeding and poor functional outcome PICO 1a In adult patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (aSAH), does treatment with antifibrinolytic drugs compared to no antifibrinolytic drugs decrease the risk of poor functional outcome? Analysis of current evidence We identified 12 RCTs comparing treatment with antifibrinolytic drugs vs no antifibrinolytic drugs, and 1 recent Cochrane review. Eleven RCTs studied the effect of tranexamic acid, and 1 trial the effect of epsilon amino-caproic acid on aneurysm rebleeding or functional outcome. Ten RCTs were performed in an era during which aneurysm treatment was postponed to the post-delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) period. In those trials, the effect of long-term treatment with antifibrinolytic drugs was studied. The 2 most recent RCTs studied the effect of short-term treatment. , The largest RCT also included patients with non-aneurysmal SAH. From that trial, we extracted data on patients with aneurysmal SAH. Pooled analyses of all available RCTs showed that treatment with antifibrinolytic drugs does not decrease the risk of poor functional outcome (odds ratio [OR]: 1.03; 95 CI, 0.86–1.23; ) or case-fatality (OR: 0.96; 95% CI, 0.81–1.15; ), despite a decreased risk of rebleeding (risk ratio [RR]: 0.56; 95% CI, 0.37–0.83; ). The discrepancy between a reduced risk of rebleeding and a neutral effect on outcome has been explained as resulting from a higher risk of ischaemic complications and hydrocephalus in patients treated with antifibrinolytic drugs, or impeded recovery from ischaemic injury. The 2 most recent RCTs were performed in an era that reflects current clinical practice with early aneurysm treatment and both microsurgical and endovascular aneurysm treatment options. , Only the Ultra-early tranexamic acid after subarachnoid haemorrhage (ULTRA) trial was adequately powered to detect a potential effect on clinical outcome. In ULTRA, tranexamic acid was started in the initial hospital directly after head CT confirmed a diagnosis of SAH. The median time between ictus and CT diagnosis was 93 min, and the time between ictus and the start of tranexamic acid was 185 min. Treatment of the ruptured aneurysm occurred after a median time of 14 h after CT diagnosis. In the 955 participants with SAH, tranexamic acid had no statistically significant effect on rebleeding (OR: 0.71; 95% CI, 0.48–1.04) and did not decrease the odds of poor functional outcome (OR: 1.16; 95% CI, 0.89–1.50) or case-fatality (OR: 1.15; 95% CI, 0.86–1.54) in the whole study population. Similar results were found in the subgroup of 813 patients with aneurysmal SAH. Although a statistically significant reduction in rebleeding was observed (OR: 0.66; 95% CI, 0.44–0.99), no effect on poor functional outcome (OR: 1.08; 95% CI, 0.82–1.43) or case-fatality (OR: 1.11; 95% CI, 0.82–1.51) was found. Short-term treatment with tranexamic acid did not increase the risk of DCI (OR: 0.99; 95% CI, 0.72–1.36) or hydrocephalus (OR: 1.23; 95% CI, 0.93–1.63). In conclusion, the ULTRA trial provided strong evidence that very early and very short-lasting antifibrinolytic therapy does not decrease the risk of poor functional outcome in patients with aSAH. Additional information After publication of the ULTRA trial, several studies were performed to investigate the effect of tranexamic acid in certain subgroups. Patients with a good clinical condition on admission and men treated with tranexamic acid had worse functional outcomes compared to those not treated with tranexamic acid. No effect on outcome was observed in patients with a poor clinical condition on admission and in women. Although the start of tranexamic acid > 6 h after ictus was associated with a reduced risk of rebleeding, it did not result in better outcomes. Analysis of current evidence We did not identify any RCTs during the last 4 decades investigating the effect of antihypertensive drugs with the primary aim of decreasing the risk of rebleeding of the ruptured aneurysm and thereby improving outcome. Additional information Several observational studies investigated the relationship between antihypertensive drug treatment and the risk of rebleeding. One study showed that blood pressure treatment may decrease the risk of rebleeding, but not poor outcome, potentially as a result of an increased risk of cerebral infarction. Additional information Several observational studies investigated the relationship between antihypertensive drug treatment and the risk of rebleeding. One study showed that blood pressure treatment may decrease the risk of rebleeding, but not poor outcome, potentially as a result of an increased risk of cerebral infarction. A study without a control group found that the incidence of rebleeding was low (3.1%) after the implementation of a strategy of intensive systolic blood pressure reduction (target 120 ± 20 mm Hg). Another study found that after the implementation of a blood pressure management protocol (systolic blood pressure target of 160 mm Hg), the incidence of in-hospital rebleeding declined from 6.7% to 2.8% (OR: 0.4; 95% CI, 0.10–1.63) and the incidence of DCI from 44.2% to 7.7% (OR: 0.10; 95% CI, 0.04–0.23). A recent study compared the incidence of in-hospital rebleeding between a hospital with a policy of aggressive blood pressure lowering (systolic blood pressure target before aneurysm treatment ≤ 140 mm Hg) vs a hospital with a more liberal blood pressure approach, and found a trend (adjusted HR 0.66 [95% CI, 0.23–1.92]) towards a lower incidence of rebleeding in the hospital with a more aggressive blood pressure lowering strategy. However, there were differences in risk factors for rebleeding between the 2 centres, which introduced major bias. PICO 2 In adult patients with aSAH, does early aneurysm occlusion compared to no early aneurysm occlusion decrease the risk of poor functional outcome? Analysis of current evidence We identified only one small RCT that assessed the timing of aneurysm treatment. The study was conducted in the pre-coiling era and included 211 good-grade (Hunt and Hess grades I–III) aSAH patients (aged 16 to 65 years) admitted to a single hospital between 1985 and 1987. Patients with intracerebral haematomas, decreased level of consciousness or severe neurological deficits were excluded. All included patients had anterior circulation aneurysms, and patients were randomly assigned to early (0–3 days), intermediate (4–7 days) or late (8 days and later) surgical clipping. Sixteen patients never underwent aneurysm surgery due to severe deterioration or death before the planned surgery. Delayed cerebral ischaemia and rebleeding were the main causes of preoperative deterioration. None of the patients received antifibrinolytic agents or hypertensive drug treatment, while intramuscular betamethasone 4 mg 4 times daily was routinely given. Of the 211 patients, 159 randomly received either intravenous followed by oral nimodipine or placebo treatment up to 21 days. The 3-month case-fatality rates were not different between early, intermediate and late surgery groups (case-fatality rates of 6%, 6% and 13%, respectively). Using a 3-point outcome scale (independent, dependent, death), 92% of the early surgery group patients were independent at 3 months, 79% in the intermediate group and 80% in the late surgery group. However, dependency was significantly higher in the intermediate surgery group (11 patients, 16%) in comparison to the early surgery group (2 patients, 3%). In summary, early surgery within 3 days after bleeding in comparison to delayed surgery did not lead to higher case-fatality. A comparison between early and intermediate surgery groups (late surgery group excluded) suggested that 3-month functional outcome was better for patients operated early. During the endovascular treatment era (since the early 1990s), no randomised trial has addressed the effect of timing of aneurysm occlusion on outcome of SAH patients. Additional information Due to the paucity of high-quality studies, recent (published within the last 10 years) meta-analyses were reviewed as supporting information. These meta-analyses generally include lower quality studies, which have inherent selection and treatment biases. In a meta-analysis including 16 observational studies of endovascular aneurysm occlusion, treatment within 24 h reduced the odds for poor outcome in comparison to patients treated at > 1 day, but not when compared to 24–72 h. A total of 26 studies with 1255 patients assessed outcomes by treatment timing. Aneurysm treatment modality PICO 3a In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of endovascular aneurysm occlusion compared to neurosurgical aneurysm occlusion decrease the risk of poor functional outcome? Analysis of current evidence A Cochrane systematic review included 4 randomised clinical trials involving 2458 participants that compared neurosurgical clipping vs endovascular coiling. The evidence in this Cochrane review comes mainly from the largest of these 4 trials (International Subarachnoid Haemorrhage Trial [ISAT]: 2143 participants). Most patients were in good clinical condition (WFNS I–III) and had an aneurysm on the anterior circulation. At 1 year after SAH, the OR of poor outcome (death or dependency) for endovascular coiling vs neurosurgical clipping was 0.69 (95% CI, 0.58–0.83; ), with an absolute risk reduction of poor outcome of 7% (95% CI, 4%–11%). The better outcome after coiling was substantiated in the worst-case-scenario analysis in which all patients lost to follow-up after coiling were given a poor outcome and those lost to follow-up after clipping a good outcome. In this worst-case scenario, the OR for poor outcome for endovascular coiling vs neurosurgical clipping was 0.74 (95% CI, 0.62–0.88; ), and the absolute risk reduction was 6% (95% CI, 2%–10%). In the subgroup of patients with a posterior circulation aneurysm (2 trials, 69 participants), the OR for poor outcome was 0.27 (95% CI, 0.09–0.82; ) and the absolute decrease in risk of poor outcome was 27% (95% CI, 6%–48%). The data from this review therefore show that coiling is associated with better clinical outcomes for patients in good clinical condition with ruptured aneurysms of either the anterior or posterior circulation that are suitable for both neurosurgical clipping and endovascular coiling. This review provides evidence of the benefit of regular endovascular coiling only, because no randomised trials were included on balloon- or stent-assisted coiling or for other endovascular procedures, such as intrasaccular devices or flow-diverting stents. Patients with middle cerebral artery (MCA) aneurysms were underrepresented in this review, and for patients with aSAH in poor clinical condition, the review found no reliable randomised evidence comparing the potential harms and benefits of endovascular coiling vs neurosurgical clipping. It must also be noted that most patients admitted to the participating hospitals at time of enrolment of the randomised trial have been treated outside the trial. The results from these trials can therefore, as for any other trial, only be extrapolated to patients fulfilling the inclusion and exclusion criteria of these trials. The overarching inclusion criterion in all these trials was equipoise for both treatment options. Long-term follow-up was available for ISAT, but not for the other trials included in the review. At 10 years, the OR of poor outcome for endovascular coiling vs neurosurgical clipping was 0.70 (95% CI, 0.56–0.88; ). Additional information One other controlled trial has been performed to compare neurosurgical clipping and endovascular treatment: the Barrow Ruptured Aneurysm Trial (BRAT). The BRAT was a single-centre clinical trial excluded from the Cochrane review due to major methodological limitations. It was not truly randomised (patients were allocated alternately), the protocol was unpublished and the trial was unregistered. Patients without aneurysms or with aneurysms unsuitable for 1 treatment were included, and 30% did not receive their assigned treatment, causing group imbalance. Missing outcomes (10%–15%) were excluded at 1 year, no intention-to-treat analyses were done after 3 years and subgroup analyses were not prespecified, leading to a very high risk of bias. At 1 year, patients assigned to coiling had better outcomes than those assigned to clipping. However, at 3, 6 and 10 years no outcome differences were found. At 10 years, complete obliteration occurred in 93% of clipped vs 22% of coiled aneurysms, with rebleeding in 2/83 coiled patients and none of the 175 clipped patients. For patients in good or moderate clinical condition (WFNS I–III) with aneurysms of either the anterior or posterior circulation that can be treated by either regular coiling or neurosurgical clipping, we have good evidence that coiling is associated with better clinical outcomes. The results of the trials cannot be generalised to the whole population of patients with ruptured aneurysms and to all endovascular and microsurgical techniques available today. For patients in a poor clinical condition and for those with an aneurysm that cannot be treated by regular coiling, there is no reliable randomised evidence comparing the potential harms and benefits of endovascular coiling vs neurosurgical clipping. In the following, we list patient populations where decisions have to be made on less robust data, based on an individual, interdisciplinary decision-making process. We here provide the data underlying our expert consensus statement. Patients in poor condition Patients with space-occupying haematomas were not included into the listed trials. This is still a patient population where the priority for microsurgical evacuation of the haematoma is the driver for the decision to rapidly operate these patients and clip the aneurysm in the same setting. Age Patients of lower age might be considered differently. Although the trials included in the Cochrane review did not specify subgroups according to age, it has been argued that the advantage of coil embolisation over clip ligation cannot be assumed for patients < 40 years old. In this age range the difference in the safety of the 2 procedures is small, and the better long-term protection from aSAH afforded by clip placement may give this treatment an advantage in life expectancy for patients < 45 years of age. Complex aneurysm morphology Patients harbouring aneurysms of complex anatomy are underrepresented in the trials. The role of the aneurysm anatomy as a driver of decision making thus remains unclear. The current evidence fails to show superiority for any treatment modality in the case of aneurysms > 10 mm, broad necked aneurysms (usually defined as neck width ≥ 4 mm or dome-to-neck ratio < 2), branching vessels arising from the aneurysm neck, fusiform aneurysms, blister aneurysms, etc. Similarly, the complexity of the aneurysm anatomy does not support the preferential use of endovascular implants other than coils over microsurgical clipping. Finally, the results obtained in the trials are limited to interdisciplinary neurovascular centres where treating physicians have sufficient experience in the treatment of these patients during the whole complex course following subarachnoid haemorrhage. PICO 3b In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of endovascular aneurysm treatment other than coiling compared to coiling of the ruptured aneurysm decrease the risk of poor functional outcome? Analysis of current evidence The trials included in the Cochrane review and BRAT compared endovascular coiling vs neurosurgical clipping. Since the implementation of coils, advanced endovascular devices, such as balloon-assisted coiling, stent-assisted coiling, flow diverting stents and intrasaccular devices, have been introduced with the aim to treat ruptured aneurysms not suited for regular coiling, eg, wide-neck aneurysms. These newer devices have enabled the endovascular repair of more complex aneurysms, but these devices also differ with respect to immediate and long-term occlusion rates as well as risks of complications, compared to coiling or microsurgical clipping. So far, only one trial has been initiated to test the superiority of endovascular management of patients with ruptured aneurysms, in which all endovascular means were included: The ISAT-2. So far, only one trial has been initiated to test the superiority of endovascular management of patients with ruptured aneurysms, in which all endovascular means were included: The ISAT-2. International Subarachnoid Haemorrhage Trial-2 was a randomised trial comparing any endovascular vs microsurgical treatment of ruptured intracranial aneurysms, focusing on those excluded from previous trials. The trial was stopped after 10 years because of slow recruitment when 270 of the 1896 planned patients had been enrolled. In total, 133 patients were randomised to microsurgical aneurysm treatment and 130 to endovascular treatment. Seven patients were excluded. This trial differed from the previous trials in the type of endovascular treatment, which was most often balloon-assisted coiling (83%). The other patients were treated with stents or flow-diverters. Moreover, 40% of the ruptured aneurysms were on the MCA, an anatomical location that was underrepresented in the previous Cochrane review. In the intention-to-treat analysis, poor outcome had occurred in 35 (27%) of 130 endovascular patients and in 40 (30%) of 133 surgical patients (RR: 0.90; 95% CI, 0.61–1.31). Residual aneurysms at 1 year were less frequent with microsurgery (10/118 [8%, 95% CI, 5%–15%]) than EVT (22/109 [20%, 95% CI, 14%–29%]). Because the trial was terminated prematurely, it lacked statistical power to rule in or out statistically significant results. Thus, for endovascular procedures other than coiling, there is no reliable evidence from randomised trials comparing these treatments vs neurosurgical clipping. Additional information Stent-assisted coiling Evidence supporting stent-assisted coiling for ruptured intracranial aneurysms remains limited and heterogeneous. A systematic review on 17 retrospective case series published before 2010 totalling 339 patients highlighted substantial variability across published case series. The pooled results suggested higher rates of complications than with regular coiling, with clinically significant intracranial haemorrhagic complications in 8% and clinically significant thromboembolic events in 6% of patients. In a subsequent systematic review and meta-analysis on 8 retrospective cohort studies with 1408 ruptured intracranial aneurysms treated before 2016, ischaemic complications occurred more often in the stent-assisted group (16.6% vs 11.0%; RR: 1.75; 95% CI, 1.3–2.36), as did haemorrhagic complications (10.3% vs 5.7%; RR: 1.6; 95% CI, 1.09–2.35), compared to regular coiling. More recent prospective multicentre registry data provide additional insight into contemporary practice. A Chinese prospective registry study reporting on 278 patients with aneurysmal SAH from wide-neck aneurysms treated with stent-assisted coiling between 2020 and 2023 found clinically relevant thromboembolic complications in 11.5% of patients and clinically relevant haemorrhagic complications in 4.7%. In conclusion, there is no good controlled evidence on stent-assisted coiling compared to regular coiling, and the observational studies suggest a high risk of complications. Balloon-assisted coiling In contrast to stent-assisted coiling, balloon remodelling does not involve permanent intravascular implants and does not require antiplatelet therapy. A meta-analysis on studies published between 1997 and 2006 reported no statistically significant differences in procedural complications between balloon-assisted and regular-unassisted coiling. However, the meta-analysis was criticised for its methodology and the exclusion of articles reporting higher complication rates. A French prospective, multicentre observational study on 768 patients treated from November 2006 to September 2008 (CLARITY) reported a significantly higher rate of adequate angiographic occlusion with balloon-assisted coiling (94.9%), compared with regular coiling (88.7%) ( P = .017), while overall rate of treatment-related complications, with or without clinical manifestations, was similar in both treatment groups (17.4% with coil embolisation and 16.9% with remodelling). Thus, good comparative and recent data on balloon-assisted coiling vs regular coiling are lacking. The few available data suggest that balloon remodelling has a safety profile comparable to regular coiling. Flow diversion Flowdiverting stents were designed for treatment of complex aneurysms, such as wide-necked sidewall aneurysms or blood blister–like aneurysms. However, they are increasingly used for other indications, eg, bifurcation aneurysms. The use of flowdiverting stents in patients with aSAH remains controversial, because they require stent deployment in the acute phase, often without adequate antiplatelet preparation, which increases the risk of thromboembolic complications. In addition, mandatory dual antiplatelet therapy increases the risk of haemorrhagic complications during necessary neurosurgical interventions (eg, external ventricular drain [EVD] placement). Because flow diversion does not immediately exclude the aneurysm from the circulation, there is a persistent risk of early rebleeding in the acute period. A meta-analysis including 20 studies (17 retrospective) published before 2018 evaluating 223 patients with acutely ruptured intracranial aneurysms treated with flow-diverter stents found that the risk of rebleeding after treatment was 4%, all occurring within 72 h after treatment. The overall risk of treatment complications was 17.8%, with the majority being ischaemic complications. Intrasaccular devices Although intrasaccular devices (also known as endosaccular flow disruptors) were specifically designed for treatment of wide-neck saccular aneurysms, there use has expanded to other indications. A meta-analysis of 16 studies published before 2024 compared the Woven EndoBridge (WEB) with either stent-assisted coiling or regular coiling, and included both studies with unruptured and ruptured intracranial aneurysms. The total risk of complications was approximately 6.5% in patients treated with WEB, compared with 14% in patients treated with stent-assisted coiling and 12% in regular coiling. The rates of adequate and complete occlusion during follow-up were similar in the 3 treatment groups, although patients treated with WEB had a shorter follow-up duration. The CLARYS study was a prospective multicentre study conducted in 13 European centres that enrolled 60 patients with a ruptured aneurysm in the anterior or posterior circulation. Twenty-three periprocedural complications occurred in 18 patients and resolved without sequelae in 16 patients. Two of these complications were attributed to the procedure and/or the use of the WEB, leading to a procedure/device-related intraoperative complication rate of 3.3%. WEB-related 1-month and 1-year morbidity and mortality were 0%. At 1 year, 19/46 aneurysms (41.3%) were completely occluded (Raymond-Roy grade I), 21/46 (45.7%) had a residual neck and 6/46 (13.0%) had residual aneurysm filling. Six patients (13%) underwent target aneurysm re-treatment within 1 year. Currently, there are no prospective long-term (>10 years) follow-up studies available with large numbers of patients and independent core lab assessments. PICO 4 In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of pharmacological or interventional treatment aiming to reduce the risk of DCI compared to no such treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome? Analysis of current evidence We systematically reviewed the literature for RCTs evaluating pharmacological and interventional strategies for DCI prevention. Only strategies investigated in at least 3 RCTs were included. In the first paragraph, we present the available evidence for calcium antagonists. Following the publication of the BRANT trial and several other RCTs, oral nimodipine became the standard of care for preventing DCI in Europe, consistent with the recommendations from previous ESO guidelines. Therefore, the subsequent paragraphs on other treatment strategies analysed only those RCTs in which patients received nimodipine as a standard of care. Pharmacological and interventional strategies were categorised based on their mechanism of action, with some categories containing a single drug and others encompassing multiple drugs with similar pharmacodynamic properties. Treatment protocols varied considerably across studies, particularly regarding dosing regimens and duration of therapy. In trials with multiple intervention arms (eg, different dosages), all intervention groups were aggregated and compared against the control group. To maintain methodological consistency, only intention-to-treat analyses from RCTs were considered. Since the current definition of DCI was standardised in 2010, earlier studies employed surrogate measures such as delayed ischaemic neurological deficits or symptomatic vasospasm. For this analysis, these outcomes were consolidated under the broader definition of DCI to enable pooling of studies. Calcium antagonists Calcium antagonists can induce vasodilation by inhibiting calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle. Therefore, calcium antagonists have been investigated for the prevention of DCI after aSAH. For our analysis, we included 7 RCTs comparing oral or intravenous (IV) nimodipine to placebo, , as well as one trial comparing nicardipine with placebo, involving a total of 2276 patients. Trials comparing different doses of nicardipine or IV nimodipine were excluded. We also reviewed 3 meta-analyses, including 1 Cochrane review, but no additional data were retrieved from these meta-analyses. Since many of these pathways are probably involved in the pathogenesis of DCI, statins have been extensively investigated in aSAH patients for DCI prevention. We identified 10 RCTs conducted between 2005 and 2020, which included a total of 1575 patients. In 6 out of 10 studies, nimodipine was administered as standard care to all patients. , , , , , Of these 6 studies, 4 investigated simvastatin, , , , 1 investigated atorvastatin, and 1 pravastatin. Magnesium sulphate Magnesium sulphate exerts pleiotropic effects, including calcium channel blockade, enhanced nitric oxide production, inhibition of NMDA receptors, reduction of inflammatory mediators and antioxidant properties. Its role as a preventive treatment for DCI has been evaluated in 13 RCTs conducted between 2002 and 2018, involving a total of 2944 patients. Each RCT used a different dosing regimen and treatment duration. Nine trials , , evaluated magnesium sulphate as an adjunct to nimodipine, comparing it with placebo plus nimodipine and therefore were included in the analysis. Seven meta-analyses were also reviewed ; however, no additional data were identified. Lumbar drainage Lumbar drainage (LD) has been investigated as a potential strategy to prevent DCI by facilitating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) removal and cisternal bloodclot wash-out downstream. Our analysis included 3 RCTs comprising 557 patients. A further meta-analysis yielded no additional data. Of the 3 RCTs, 1 reported functional outcome using means and medians of GOS scores at 1- and 3-month follow-up, instead of proportions of patients with poor outcome. The corresponding author was contacted multiple times for more information but did not respond. Therefore, that trial could not be included in the meta-analysis. Instead, the results of that trial are reported separately. Analysis of current evidence Endovascular treatment of vasospasm in aSAH—such as intra-arterial pharmacological therapy and mechanical vasodilatation using balloon angioplasty or temporary deployment of a retrievable stent—has been explored in clinical studies as a potential strategy to treat DCI. Two RCTs on the effects of endovascular treatment of vasospasm in aSAH patients with DCI have been completed to date. , An RCT in 3 German centres was stopped prematurely for safety reasons after a prespecified interim analysis, when 36 out of the planned 92 patients were randomised. Eighteen patients were randomised to endovascular treatment and 18 to the control arm. Two patients in the intervention arm did not receive endovascular treatment and were not included in the analysis. Of the 16 patients who underwent endovascular treatment, 5 patients received 1 treatment, 7 patients 2 treatments, 2 patients 3 treatments, 1 patient 4 treatments and 1 patient 5 treatments. The majority of procedures (29/34) consisted of intra-arterial nimodipine and 4/34 procedures were done by balloon angioplasty. Five out of 34 (15%) endovascular treatment procedures resulted in major treatment complications (2 dissections, 3 infarctions). No effect on the primary endpoint (incidence of new infarct lesions measured on diffusion weighted MR images) was observed. Patients randomised to the control arm had a better clinical outcome at 6 months than patients randomised to endovascular treatment of vasospasm (mRS 2 ± 1.5 vs 4 ± 1.8; P = .004). A systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 non-randomised, predominantly retrospective cohort studies (517 patients) compared endovascular therapy (intra-arterial pharmacological treatment with or without balloon angioplasty) with the standard treatment for vasospasm after aSAH. A multicentre retrospective cohort study from 3 US academic centres evaluated the safety and efficacy of non-compliant balloon angioplasty for vasospasm after aSAH. Fifty-two patients were included who had new focal or global neurologic deficits resulting from DCI in combination with moderate or severe angiographic vasospasm. In total, 165 angioplasty procedures were performed. The study did not include a control group. The main outcomes were angiographic improvement of vasospasm, delayed cerebral infarction on CT or MRI and functional outcome (mRS). Angiographic improvement occurred in 97% of treated vessels, and clinical symptoms improved in 78.8% of patients. Cerebral infarction developed in 46.2% of patients, and 61.5% achieved favourable functional outcome (mRS 0–2) at follow-up. No procedure-related complications were reported. The authors concluded that non-compliant balloon angioplasty appears safe and effective in improving angiographic vasospasm in patients with medically refractory vasospasm. However, in the absence of a control group, no conclusion can be made on the effect on functional outcome. A single-centre retrospective observational study evaluated the effect of distal balloon angioplasty for vasospasm after aSAH. The study included 392 patients treated between 2012 and 2017. Between 2012 and 2015, 160 patients received proximal balloon angioplasty, if needed followed by intra-arterial pharmacological therapy for distal vasospasm. From 2015 to 2017, 232 patients received proximal balloon angioplasty, if needed followed by distal balloon angioplasty. The primary endpoint was delayed cerebral infarction occurring in the territory of a previously treated vessel. Distal balloon angioplasty was associated with lower rates of post-angioplasty delayed cerebral infarction (2.2% vs 7.5%) and fewer repeat angioplasty procedures (8% vs 19%). However, overall delayed cerebral infarction, mortality and favourable functional outcome did not differ significantly between treatment periods. Procedure-related complications were uncommon, with angioplasty-related infarction in ~ 2.5% and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage in ~ 0.7%–1.3%. The authors concluded that distal balloon angioplasty may reduce angiographic recurrence of vasospasm and post-angioplasty infarction but did not demonstrate a clear clinical benefit. Finally, temporary deployment of retrievable stents has been reported in small observational series as a mechanical approach for vasospasm treatment. However, since the available studies were limited to small uncontrolled cohorts, none of the studies adhered to the inclusion criteria for this guideline. In conclusion, the available evidence for endovascular treatment of vasospasm is predominantly observational and retrospective. Adequately powered, randomised controlled clinical trials with predefined clinical endpoints are urgently needed to answer the question whether endovascular treatment of vasospasm in patients with DCI is safe and decreases the risk of poor functional outcome after aSAH. Other hypotheses for the pathogenesis of DCI include microthrombosis, microcirculatory spasm, cortical spreading ischaemia and impaired cerebral autoregulation. In addition, clinical trials showed that treatment strategies that reduce macrovascular spasm do not decrease the risk of poor functional outcome, which questions the usefulness of detecting angiographic vasospasm. , Perfusion imaging Imaging of brain perfusion may detect tissue at risk for irreversible ischaemic damage and guide therapeutic interventions. Due to its practicability and favourable risk/benefit profile for aSAH patients, CTP measurement evolved as the most used perfusion imaging modality. CTP combines information about macro- and microvascular blood flow and may distinguish between reversible hypoperfusion and irreversible ischaemia. Quantitative image analyses with calculation of CBF, cerebral blood volume, mean transit time (MTT), time to peak and time to drain have been used to investigate impaired brain perfusion in aSAH patients. Increase in MTT has repeatedly been reported to accurately predict DCI before irreversible ischaemia occurs. In a prospective cohort of 64 aSAH patients with quantitative CTP at day 3, MTT predicted DCI with a sensitivity of 95% (95% CI, 83%–99%) and a negative predictive value of 96% (95% CI, 87%–99%) indicating very high diagnostic accuracy as screening tool for DCI. , In a meta-analysis of 570 patients, a decrease of CBF (pooled mean difference − 11.9 mL/100 g per minute [95% CI, −15.2 to −8.6]) and an increase in MTT (pooled mean difference 1.5 s [CI, 0.9–2.2]) during the high-risk phase (days 4–14 after ictus) was associated with DCI. However, absolute values of quantitative CTP parameters vary between different CT scanners and analysis algorithms. Therefore, measuring perfusion by CTP needs standardisation to define generalisable absolute perfusion thresholds after aSAH in future studies. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Although MRI is a sensitive modality for the early detection of cerebral ischaemia, its feasibility in the routine management of patients with aSAH during the high-risk period for DCI is limited by both patient-related and logistical factors. Many patients with aSAH are restless or have a decreased level of consciousness and therefore unable to lie still, which makes an MRI scan impossible. Furthermore, having a patient on the respiratory machine for about 20 min and monitoring that patient in the MR suite is challenging and often undesirable. In addition, when ischaemic lesions are detected on MRI, it is often difficult to determine whether these findings are attributable to DCI, acute ischaemic events (resulting from the acute aneurysm rupture) or procedure-related ischaemia. Collectively, these considerations limit the utility of MRI as a diagnostic tool in routine clinical practice. Emerging technologies, such as bedside ultra-low-field portable MRI systems and further reductions in acquisition time, may help to address some of these limitations in the future. Analysis of current evidence The literature search yielded no randomised trials or otherwise controlled studies, but only uncontrolled observational studies, which are discussed in the additional information section. Additional information Transcranial Doppler TCD Transcranial Doppler is widely used for routine monitoring of arterial blood flow velocities as an indirect measure to detect large artery vasospasm after aSAH. The non-invasive nature and bedside availability of TCD offer advantages over other imaging modalities for vasospasm monitoring. However, as discussed above, there is ongoing debate about the clinical relevance of macrovascular spasm and elevated blood flow velocities in cerebral arteries measured by TCD. , A meta-analysis of 15 studies comparing TCD with DSA for detection of angiographic vasospasm in the middle cerebral artery reported a pooled sensitivity of 66.7% (95% CI, 55.9–75.9) and specificity of 89.5% (95% CI, 80.3–94.7). An estimated vasospasm incidence of 70% in aSAH patients results in a positive predictive value of 93.7% and negative predictive value of 53.4%. Due to even lower negative predictive values for all other cerebral arteries, TCD does not reliably exclude the presence of vasospasm. The limited diagnostic accuracy of TCD, and the fact that most patients with large artery vasospasm do not have clinical deterioration due to DCI undermines its usefulness as a reliable screening tool in the monitoring of aSAH patients. Continuous EEG In unconscious patients, subtle neurological changes caused by focal cerebral ischaemia are often difficult to recognise. Continuous EEG (cEEG) may partially compensate for missing functional information. cEEG can be used for monitoring seizure activity and brain function in critically ill patients with altered mental status. In aSAH patients, seizure activity in cEEG has been reported in up to 19% of patients, which may contribute to worse clinical outcome. In addition to seizure detection, cEEG data can be analysed to define patterns of DCI-related pathological electric activity of the brain. For example, a decreased alpha to delta ratio is associated with DCI. In a prospective study of 227 consecutive aSAH patients, 103 were eligible for quantitative EEG analyses. In this cohort, cEEG predicted DCI with a sensitivity of 91% (95% CI, 81%–98%) and specificity of 83% (95% CI, 71%–93%) in low-risk patients, and a sensitivity of 95% (95% CI, 87%–99%) and specificity of 77% (95% CI, 36%–99%) in high-risk patients. However, the identified EEG patterns for DCI prediction and diagnosis need further validation in independent cohorts of aSAH patients with standardised definitions. In addition, clinical trials are needed to investigate whether therapeutic interventions based on cEEG findings decrease the risk of poor functional outcome in aSAH patients, to justify the high resource requirements for around-the-clock real-time data acquisition and interpretation. Invasive neuromonitoring probes Parenchymal monitoring probes can be used to obtain additional physiological data in neurologically unassessable aSAH patients, eg, ICP, regional CBF and the metabolic status of the brain. Intracranial pressure elevations are common and have been reported in up to 80% of poor grade aSAH patients. In unconscious patients with radiographic signs of hydrocephalus, ICP can be reliably monitored via an EVD (also see PICO 7). However, there is uncertainty about the risk/benefit profile of EVD insertion for ICP monitoring in aSAH patients without radiographic hydrocephalus. Parenchymal ICP probes are considered less invasive and commonly used for this indication. The SYNAPSE-ICU study was an international, prospective observational cohort study of 2395 patients with acute brain injury, of whom 521 (22%) had SAH, , which aimed to explore practice variation in ICP monitoring variation to prioritise uncertainties in the clinical management of critical care patients with acute brain injury and support further collaborative prospective studies. The study showed that SAH patients with ICP monitoring received more aggressive therapy treatments compared to patients without ICP monitoring. Intracranial pressure monitoring was associated with a reduction in poor functional outcome (OR: 0.14; 95% CI, 0.02–0.53) and case-fatality (HR: 0.25; 95% CI, 0.13–0.49) in SAH patients in a poor clinical condition, but not in those with 2 reactive pupils. Combined probes allow for continuous measurement of brain tissue oxygen pressure (PtbO 2 ) and ICP. This, in combination with systemic blood pressure measurements, may provide information about cerebral autoregulation. Brain tissue oxygen pressure monitoring has been reported to be sensitive in detection of metabolic cerebral compromise even in the absence of elevated ICP. In addition, microdialysis with quantification of interstitial metabolites, such as lactate and pyruvate, have been reported to detect metabolic derangements in situations without impaired PtbO 2 . Treatment paradigms for poor grade aSAH patients based on an extended definition of DCI integrating multimodal neuromonitoring data (ICP, PtbO 2 , microdialysis) have been reported to increase 12 months favourable neurological outcome in a cohort of 55 consecutive poor grade aSAH patients. However, due to the very limited sample size of reported neuromonitoring studies in aSAH patients, inconsistent definitions of DCI across studies, the lack of validated clinically relevant thresholds and limited therapeutic options, there is uncertainty about the risk/benefit profile of invasive monitoring methods. In addition, invasive multimodal neuromonitoring is inherently limited by providing only regional information around the site of implantation and a lack of data from clinical good grade aSAH patients. Additional information EVD in acute hydrocephalus after aSAH The placement of an EVD in patients with acute hydrocephalus following aSAH, whether obstructive or communicating, is common practice in nearly all centres treating aSAH patients. External ventricular drain allows rapid control of acute hydrocephalus and ICP, and thereby is often considered a lifesaving treatment. In case of obstructive hydrocephalus or significant mass effect it is the only treatment possible, since LD or LP in these situations can lead to death by brain herniation. However, although commonly performed, EVD also has specific risks: brain haemorrhage along the catheter tract, catheter malposition, mechanical brain injury with putative long-term effect on motor function, cognition and risk of seizures, as well as catheter-related infection. , In addition, there is a debate regarding the indications for EVD placement, which can be clinical (decreased level of consciousness) and/or radiological (ventricular enlargement). Therefore, the risk/benefit ratio of EVD insertion must be weighed and alternatives considered. LD and LP in acute hydrocephalus after aSAH In case of acute and communicating hydrocephalus, a LD or LP can also be used instead of an EVD. Placement of an LD or performance of an LP probably carries a lower risk of complications than the placement of an EVD. However, CSF diversion by means of a LD or LP in case of obstructive hydrocephalus or significant cerebral oedema poses a risk of tonsillar herniation and thus death, and is therefore contraindicated in these situations. Regarding the LD, an observational study without control group reported no complications related to LD insertion (infection, brain herniation, over drainage) in 28 Fisher III aSAH patients. In another study, 229 Fisher III aSAH patients without obstructive hydrocephalus had an LD inserted, and the rate of CSF infection was 0.4%, which may be lower than that observed with EVD. One study in aSAH patients with symptomatic hydrocephalus retrospectively compared 56 patients with an EVD and 21 patients with a LD. The decision to treat with EVD or LD depended on the surgeon on call. Overall drain complications were 32.0% in patients with EVD and 9.5% in patients with LD. External ventricular drain vs LD complications consisted of haemorrhage (1.8% vs 0%), infection (7.1 vs 0%), clogged drain (25% vs 0%), dislodgement of drain (1.8% vs 4.6%) and replacement of drain (16% vs 4.8%). No case of cerebellar tonsillar herniation occurred. Regarding LP, in an observational study, 17 patients with symptomatic communicating hydrocephalus were treated by serial LPs. None had CSF infection or tonsillar herniation, and none required EVD insertion. In a recent study, 86 patients with aSAH and acute symptomatic hydrocephalus were treated with LP as initial treatment. Seventy patients (81%) showed initial improvement after initial LP, 39 (45%) improved with LP only and 41 (48%) needed continuous drainage by LD or EVD. Thus, LD or EVD insertion could be avoided in approximately half of the patients. The rate of complications related to LP was not explicitly reported. This question has been investigated in several observational studies. Regarding EVD, a meta-analysis of observational studies reported rebleeding among 106/960 patients (11%) treated with EVD, vs 250/2711 patients without EVD (9.2%; OR: 1.60, 95% CI, 0.82–3.22). However, several confounding factors limit the interpretation of these findings, particularly the time interval between ictus, EVD placement, rebleeding and aneurysm treatment. Another study compared 3 matched patient groups: those with hydrocephalus treated with EVD, those with hydrocephalus without EVD and those without hydrocephalus ( n = 34 per group). The mean time from ictus to CSF drainage was 12 h, and drainage continued for an average of 6.3 days prior to aneurysm treatment. Rebleeding rates were similar across groups, occurring in 7/34 patients in both hydrocephalus groups and in 6/34 patients in the group without hydrocephalus. These findings suggest that early EVD placement with prolonged CSF drainage does not appear to increase the risk of rebleeding. Although EVD itself may not increase rebleeding risk, another study with 194 patients suggested that not EVD by itself, but rather the volume and timing of CSF drainage (60 mL of CSF drained in 6 h) may increase the risk of rebleeding. This observation indicates that the risk may be related to both the volume and timing of CSF drainage. Regarding LD, in a retrospective study, rebleeding occurred in 11/324 (3.4%) patients with LD and in 2/51 (3.9%) patients without LD. Permanent CSF shunt in aSAH There are no high-quality studies evaluating the benefit of placing a permanent shunt in chronic hydrocephalus following aSAH. Insertion of permanent shunt is proposed when the EVD or LD cannot be removed, or in case of symptomatic chronic hydrocephalus. When an external drain has been inserted (EVD or LD), the removal of this drain usually relies on a clamping attempt with clinical and radiological assessment. The duration of external drainage that necessitates the placement of an internal shunt is unknown, as well as the number of failures of drain closure indicating the insertion of a permanent CSF shunt. Of note, the longer the EVD is inserted, the higher the risk of catheter-related infection is. Chronic hydrocephalus after aSAH may also become clinically manifest after the removal of the external drain, several weeks after discharge. A retrospective study that included 39 patients provides controlled data. Patients presenting with gait ataxia, cognitive disturbance and urinary incontinence had enlarged ventricles and normal CSF opening pressure on LP. Patients with high CSF opening pressure were excluded. Of the remaining participants, 24 received a VP shunt and 15 did not receive a VP shunt. At 1 and 6 months, Barthel index scores (39 vs 47) and Mini Mental Status (18 vs 19) were improved in the VP shunt group. In a single centre retrospective North American study the implementation of a neurointensivist co-management approach in a neurosurgical ICU (296 aSAH patients admitted between 2005 and 2007 compared to a historical control group of 216 aSAH patients admitted between 2003 and 2005) did not show an effect on hospital mortality (18.2% after vs 13.4% before [ P = .14]), although there was a statistically significant decrease of mean length of ICU stay (from 12.4 days to 10.9 days, P = .02) and of the need for VP shunts (23.0% vs 11.5% [ P = .001]). In a single-centre North-American study including 363 SAH patients among a mixed cohort of 2096 stroke patients, availability of a neurocritical care specialist, but not a specialised neurocritical care units was associated with improved discharge disposition, lower in-hospital mortality (48/259 [18.5%] vs 33/104 [31.7%]; P = .006), or withdrawal of care, and lower mortality at 3 months (52/259 [20.1%] vs 33/104 [31.7%]; P = .018) and 12 months (54/259 [20.8%] vs 35/104 [33.7%]; P = .01) specifically in aSAH patients. When the trained neurointensivist left the unit and was not replaced, a greater rate of in-hospital mortality or discharge to hospice (OR: 2.206 [95% CI, 1.062–4.584]; P = .034), overall worsened discharge disposition (OR: 2.455 [95% CI, 1.165–5.177]; P = .018) and shorter ICU LOS (OR: 0.459 [95% CI, 0.229–0.917]; P = .028) was observed. In a European study, the effect of the implementation of a neurocritical care protocol was studied among microsurgically clipped aSAH patients ( n = 198, admitted between 1999 and 2003) compared to historical controls ( n = 150, 1993–1994). The latter group included a significantly higher percentage of severe aSAH patients (WFNS grades IV and V) compared to the historical group (47.0% vs 15.3%, P < .0001) and WFNS grade V patients were not treated in the historical control group. While overall outcomes were similar, the study showed significant improvement for the most severe cases. In the historical group, all patients with WFNS grade V died or survived in a vegetative state, as they were not treated with aneurysm surgery. In contrast, 35.1% of WFNS grade V patients in the latter group (20 out of 57 patients) achieved a good functional outcome. The authors concluded that specialised neurocritical care is particularly beneficial for patients with high-grade aSAH. Contrarily, a German study included 755 aSAH patients (456 in a neurosurgical ICU, 2005–2013 vs 299 in a general ICU, 1990–2005), found that the type of ICU was neither associated with discharge GOS nor 6-month GOS (OR: 1.45 [95% CI, 0.53–3.95]) for long-term outcome. In a North-American study the implementation of a neurointensivist team ( n = 108 aSAH patients admitted between 1998 and 2000) was neither associated with NICU mortality (HR 1.39 [95% CI, 0.67–2.88]) nor in-hospital mortality (HR 1.48 [95% CI, 0.65–3.34]). However, NICU and hospital length of stay were significantly reduced (HR 1.60 [95% CI, 1.13–2.26] and HR 1.43 [95% CI, 1.01–2.03]). Due to limitations in study design—primarily retrospective observational studies with historical control groups—along with changes in clinical care over time, variations in pre-hospital management and differences in the timing of aneurysm treatment, the impact of specialised neurocritical care on patient outcomes is likely multifactorial. Higher levels of evidence can only be achieved through prospective randomised trials. Topic 9. Centre volume and number/volume of neurosurgeon and neurointerventionalist PICO 9a In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment in a high-volume centre compared to a low-volume centre decrease the risk of poor functional outcome ? Analysis of current evidence The literature search found no randomised or otherwise controlled trials, but only retrospective or registry-based studies, which are discussed in the additional information section. Additional information We found 2 systematic reviews analysing studies on the relationship between hospital case volume and in-hospital mortality. The first review included studies published up to 2012 assessing the relationship between hospital caseload and in-hospital mortality for patients undergoing treatment after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. This review included 4 studies, describing 36,600 patients. The quality of studies was graded as low in 3 and very low in 1. A meta-analysis using a random effects model showed a decrease in hospital mortality (OR: 0.77 [95% CI, 0.60–0.97]) in high-volume hospitals treating SAH patients. Removal of the study with very low quality increased the effect size (OR: 0.68 [95% CI, 0.56–0.84]). The definition of hospital volume differed among studies. In one study, low volume was defined as 9 or fewer patients per year, whereas in another, it was defined as fewer than 30 patients per year. Similarly, one study defined high volume as more than 20 patients annually, and another defined it as more than 50 patients a year. Apart from the non-uniform cut-off values for low- or high-volume centres, there was also uncertainty about the case-mix between centres, and no adjustment for baseline characteristics was not performed. The second systematic review included studies that reported in-hospital mortality in SAH patients and provided an adjusted OR or core data on baseline characteristics, such as age, sex and co-morbidities, to calculate an adjusted OR. The 5 included studies were published between 2002 and 2019; 4 were of high methodological quality according to the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, and the fifth had a moderate quality. Three studies came from Asia, and 2 from Europe and the United States. In total, the 5 studies enrolled 46,186 patients. Crude in-hospital mortality ranged from 7.0% to 40%. High hospital case volume was associated with reduced in-hospital mortality (OR: 0.53; 95% CI, 0.42–0.68). This association was found in each included study separately, and was consistent in subgroups divided according to geographical region, treatment modality (surgical vs endovascular), proportion of surgical patients, sample size and annualised case volume grouping. Studies dichotomised the annualised case volumes, or divided these into tertiles or quartiles, with the highest categories starting at 19, 30, 70 or 100 patients per year. For one study, the cut-offs were not reported. We also found one study that did not use in-hospital data for outcome assessment, but mortality at 1 year after SAH. This study was based on registries of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, and included 5773 SAH patients and 1807 patients with unruptured aneurysms admitted between 2002 and 2010 in 15 neurosurgical centres. It used population-based death registries for outcome assessment in patients with SAH and unruptured intracranial aneurysms. For case volume load, the centres were divided into 3 tertiles (with < 36 patients per year in the lowest tertile and > 63 in the highest tertile). One-year mortality in patients with aSAH was slightly higher with increasing case load (HR per 10-patient increase, 1.04; 95% CI, 1.00–1.07) after adjusting for several baseline factors, but not SAH severity. One of the potential explanations for these discrepant results that the authors provide is that, in these Scandinavian countries, all treatments of intracranial aneurysms are performed at academic hospitals by specialised cerebrovascular surgeons and interventional neuroradiologists. In contrast to the somewhat worse outcome after SAH in high volume centres, however, there was a trend towards better outcome for treatment of unruptured aneurysms in high volume centres in this study, which is not in line with this potential explanation. Others have argued that the worse outcome in high-volume centres is explained by selection bias, with high-volume centres accepting patients in poor clinical condition more often, and thus at higher risk of poor outcome. In conclusion, there is high consistency between studies regarding a positive relationship between hospital caseload and in-hospital outcomes. Also, throughout the range of criteria for high-volume centres, there is consistency regarding high case volume and in-hospital favourable outcomes. This relation remains even if the cut-off for high volume is based on high caseloads, such as 70 or even 100 patients per year. In addition, these studies should aim to determine the optimal volume threshold for defining a centre as high-volume. PICO 9b In adult patients with aSAH, does aneurysm treatment by a high-volume neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist, compared to a low-volume neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist, decrease the risk of poor functional outcome? Analysis of current evidence The literature search found no controlled studies. Additional information For several common procedures, such as carotid endarterectomy, coronary artery bypass grafting, valve replacement and abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, surgeon specialisation is an important predictor of operative mortality independent of volume in that specific procedure. The literature search revealed no such data on intracranial aneurysm repair. We found one study that investigated the association between the neurosurgeon’s scientific productivity and clinical outcomes following microsurgical clipping of ruptured aneurysms. The study was a post-hoc analysis of 3307 patients from 162 centres in 21 countries, who had undergone clipping of ruptured intracranial aneurysms by 147 neurosurgeons and who had participated in drug trials between 1990 and 1997. In this single study, patients under the care of neurosurgeons with higher H-indices had better functional outcomes ( P = 0.01) compared to neurosurgeons with lower H-indices, without any statistically significant difference in mortality. Neither the total number of publications nor possession of a graduate degree had an impact on outcomes. In the ESO guidelines on unruptured intracranial aneurysms it was suggested to repair unruptured intracranial aneurysms only in centres performing the proposed treatment in > 30 patients with (ruptured or unruptured) aneurysms per year per neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist. PICO 10 In adult patients with aSAH, does radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment, compared to a maximum radiological follow-up duration of 6 months, decrease the risk of poor functional outcome? Analysis of current evidence There are no completed RCTs or prospective cohort studies investigating whether radiological follow-up beyond 6 months in adult patients with aSAH decreases the risk of poor functional outcome, compared to radiological follow-up only until 6 months after aneurysm treatment. Additional information In the current literature, relevant studies are limited to the assessment of radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment in adult patients with aSAH. There are no studies available addressing radiological follow-up within 6 months after aneurysm treatment for comparison. Recanalisation Recanalisation of a treated aneurysm can occur at different stages with everything beyond 6 months being labelled as late recanalisation. Data on late recanalisation stem from non-randomised, uncontrolled studies, which show high heterogeneity in follow-up duration, follow-up modality, definition of recanalisation and rupture status of the aneurysm, limiting the generalisability of the studies. A study enrolling 435 aSAH survivors after clipping, with a total follow-up time of 5681 patient-years found a probability of 0.7% of re-occurrence within 10 years for patients without a residual neck immediately after treatment, compared to 13.9% in patients with a neck remnant. These results were confirmed by a recent meta-analysis including 1167 patients (463 with ruptured aneurysms) treated first line with the smart coil device, which showed a late recanalisation rate of 10% (95% CI, 6%–17%). For the WEB device, late recanalisation rates of 11% and 11.5% were reported, , while for flow-diverters, rates of adequate occlusion were higher at 12 months compared to 6 months and ranged between 77% and 92%. A WEB database study evaluating 763 patients, of whom 230 had treatment of a ruptured intracranial aneurysm, found an occlusion rate of 65.1% during a mean follow-up duration of 17.7 months, with 7.3% of the patients requiring re-treatment. On multivariate analysis, independent factors negatively correlated with complete aneurysm occlusion at the last follow-up were being a former smoker(OR: 0.5; 95% CI, 0.3–0.8), maximal aneurysm diameter (OR: 0.8; 95% CI, 0.7–0.8) and the presence of an aneurysm wall branch (OR: 0.4; 95% CI, 0.28–0.73). Recurrent SAH The best available evidence on long-term risk of recurrent aSAH (either from the target aneurysm, another aneurysm at baseline or from a de novo aneurysm after aSAH) comes from the ISAT trial which followed the UK cohort for 18 years. In this cohort, the risk of recurrent aSAH between 30

patients requiring re-treatment. On multivariate analysis, independent factors negatively correlated with complete aneurysm occlusion at the last follow-up were being a former smoker(OR: 0.5; 95% CI, 0.3–0.8), maximal aneurysm diameter (OR: 0.8; 95% CI, 0.7–0.8) and the presence of an aneurysm wall branch (OR: 0.4; 95% CI, 0.28–0.73). Recurrent SAH The best available evidence on long-term risk of recurrent aSAH (either from the target aneurysm, another aneurysm at baseline or from a de novo aneurysm after aSAH) comes from the ISAT trial which followed the UK cohort for 18 years. In this cohort, the risk of recurrent aSAH between 30 days and 1 year was 0.6% in the coiling group and 0.4% in the clipping group; between 1 and 5 years, it was 0.021% and 0.006% and after 5 years, it was 0.5% and 0.3%, respectively. For the target aneurysm, the risk of recurrent aSAH was 1.6% in the coiling group and 0.5% in the clipping group suggesting a very limited clinical impact of prolonged surveillance. It may be that these numbers are an underestimation, since re-treatment may have prevented recurrent aSAH. In the long-term follow-up study, no data on follow-up imaging and re-treatment were available. On the other hand, in the era that ISAT was performed, re-treatment was rarely conducted. We retrieved additional data from uncontrolled cohort studies. One study reported on 1001 patients with aSAH treated with coil or clip in 9 high-volume centres in the United States from 1996 to 1998. During a mean follow-up of 4 years, 19 post-procedural re-ruptures occurred. This study suggests a strong correlation of re-rupture risk and initial occlusion rate with higher rate of re-rupture in initially incompletely occluded aneurysms (overall risk: 1.1% for complete occlusion, 2.9% for 91%–99% occlusion, 5.9% for 70%–90%, 17.6% for < 70%; P < .0001 in univariate and multivariable analysis). In addition, long-term follow-up data (mean 73.7 months) from a single-centre study including 570 patients with coil embolisation after aSAH suggests a rate of late re-rupture (defined as > 30 days after treatment) of 1.6%, which is in line with the ISAT data. De novo aneurysm formation De novo aneurysm formation is a second reason for extended follow-up. Studies on this topic are limited by incomplete follow-up, varying imaging modalities and a lack of standardisation in timing of imaging. This limits our understanding of the true rates of recurrence and/or re-rupture, particularly with the use of newer endovascular devices. A meta-analysis from 2018 including patients with and without SAH reported the overall incidence of de novo aneurysm formation of 2% (95% CI, 2%–3%) over a mean follow-up time of 8.3 years. If a de novo aneurysm was found, 11.2% were detected in the first 5 years, and the majority (88.8%) after more than 5 years. This study did not find a statistically significant difference in rates of de novo aneurysm formation between patients who had ruptured aneurysms and those with unruptured aneurysms. A recent meta-analysis including 9351 patients from 19 cohort studies published between 1993 and 2021 found that during a follow-up period of 2.5–18.5 years, 304 (3.25%) patients developed a de novo aneurysm. Main risk factors were age < 60 years (RR: 1.41; 95% CI, 1.25–1.58), female sex (RR: 1.63; 95% CI, 1.27–2.08), smoking history (RR: 1.37; 95% CI, 1.07–1.80), family history of IAs (RR: 2.30; 95% CI, 1.32–4.00) and multiple IAs at initial diagnosis (RR: 1.69; 95% CI, 1.11–2.58). In this paper a prediction model from those studies was developed. This prediction model showed an increasing risk for de novo aneurysms with an increasing risk score resulting in a 25% risk at scores of 16–23. Another study supported these risk factors and found that stage 3 or greater chronic kidney disease in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease as an additional risk factor for de novo aneurysms. Different follow-up modalities must be used for microsurgical or endovascular therapy. As clips result in severe artefacts on MRI, only DSA or CTA are suitable for detecting recanalisation or a growing aneurysm remnant at the treated location. MRA is only useful for the detection of new aneurysms at other locations not affected by clip-related artefacts. In conclusion, these data indicate that (progressive) recanalisation and recurrent SAH of a treated aneurysm or de novo aneurysm may occur beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment. However, a beneficial effect of radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment on outcome has not been established. Most aneurysms with recanalisation will not rupture during a patient’s lifetime, while re-treatment carries a risk of complications that may affect outcome. It remains unclear whether the beneficial effect on prevention of recurrent aSAH outweighs the risk of complications from re-treatment. Discussion We used the GRADE methodology to develop evidence-based recommendations and formulated expert consensus statements in areas of uncertainty to assist physicians in decision-making regarding patients with aSAH. All 15 evidence-based recommendations and 37 expert consensus statements are summarised in . Full consensus among the voting MWG members was obtained on 16 expert consensus statements, and a majority agreed on the other 21 statements. This ESO/EANS/ESMINT guideline on aSAH expands upon previous guidelines from the European Stroke Organisation (2013), American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (2023), and Neurocritical Care Society (2023). The 2013 ESO guideline addressed the management of both unruptured intracranial aneurysms and subarachnoid haemorrhage. In 2022, the ESO guideline was updated for unruptured intracranial aneurysms. Only a few evidence-based recommendations in this guideline are supported by high-level evidence. These include the use of oral nimodipine (PICO 4) and treatment of the ruptured aneurysm by regular coiling when both regular coiling and microsurgical clipping are equally suitable in patients who are in a good clinical condition (PICO 3). In addition, there were evidence-based recommendations with a moderate level of evidence against giving antifibrinolytic drugs (PICO 1), tirilazad, statins, magnesium sulphate, or ETRAs (all PICO 4). There was a low level of evidence for the routine use of lumbar drains (PICO 4). Although 3 RCTs were performed investigating the effect of LD, we could only include data from 2 RCTs in a pooled analysis on functional outcome and concluded that no recommendation could be made on the routine use of lumbar drains until more RCT data become available. Also for PICO 5, there was a low-level of evidence. This is particularly noteworthy given the widespread clinical use of rescue therapy (induced hypertension or endovascular treatment of vasospasm) in patients who develop DCI. Similarly, there was a very low-level of evidence for the use of endovascular techniques and devices other than regular coiling for the treatment of the ruptured aneurysm, despite their widespread use. In areas where more guidance was needed, expert consensus statements were developed to support clinical decision-making in routine practice. One of the major differences from the previous ESO guideline is that we now address the use of balloon-assisted coiling, intrasaccular devices, stent-assisted coiling and flow-diverting stents for the treatment of the ruptured aneurysm. Although the ISAT trial demonstrated that regular coiling is superior to microsurgical clipping for (small neck) ruptured aneurysms that are equally suitable for both approaches, it is often assumed that advanced endovascular techniques offer a similar advantage over microsurgical clipping. However, this assumption has not been confirmed in an RCT. Studies in unruptured intracranial aneurysms show that stent-assisted coiling and flowdiverting stents are associated with a higher risk of treatment complications compared to regular coiling. The ISAT-2 trial compared any endovascular treatment (>80% treated by balloon-assisted coiling) with microsurgical treatment of the ruptured intracranial aneurysm, but the trial was prematurely terminated because of poor enrolment and was therefore underpowered to draw strong conclusions. The literature on endovascular treatment options for intracranial aneurysms primarily consists of case series or registries, most of which are retrospective or sponsored by industry, and the few comparative studies mostly have a non-randomised design. The only randomised comparison was severely underpowered because it was stopped prematurely when only 14% of the patients needed were included. The available studies also have other methodological flaws. In a systematic review of 1356 studies with 410,993 patients, key outcomes were rarely clearly defined and were often incompletely reported. A definition for safety was provided in only 2% of studies, and only 0.1% specified a complication, mortality or morbidity rate below which a procedure would qualify as safe. Definitions of effectiveness were similarly uncommon: only 2% addressed this outcome at the aneurysm level, and none defined a threshold for ineffectiveness. Another review evaluating flow-diverting stents for unruptured intracranial aneurysms reported industry involvement or conflicts of interest in 7 of 13 studies, highlighting the potential for bias in the published outcomes. We recommend investigator-initiated RCTs in which the safety, efficacy and durability of new devices are compared with existing treatment options, with predefined outcomes that are assessed by independent outcome assessors without industry involvement.
